questions.q: A flat order_sheet table repeats each customer's phone on every order row. Support changes Ada's phone on one of her orders only. Which problem is this?
questions.explain: The phone is one fact stored once per order row. Changing some copies and not others leaves the data contradicting itself. Normalising moves the phone into customers, where it is stored once.
options: An update anomaly: one fact stored in several rows, and the update missed some of them
An insertion anomaly: a new fact cannot be stored without another one
A deletion anomaly: deleting one fact removes another
A lost update: two sessions overwrote each other

questions.q: In the flat sheet keyed by (order_id, sku), why can't the shop record a new product that nobody has ordered yet?
questions.explain: That is an insertion anomaly. The product's facts depend on sku alone, but they are stored in a table whose key also needs an order. Giving products their own table removes it.
options: Because sku is not unique in the sheet
Because a product only exists as part of an order row, and order_id is part of the primary key, so it cannot be null
Because PostgreSQL forbids tables with more than seven columns in a primary key
Because the price column has no default

questions.q: A table order_lines (order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name) has the key (order_id, product_id). Which normal form does it break, and why?
questions.explain: A partial dependency on part of a composite key breaks 2NF. The fix is to drop product_name and join to products.
options: 1NF, because product_name is text
2NF, because product_name depends on only part of the key (product_id)
3NF, because quantity depends on product_name
None: every column is atomic, so it is fully normalised

questions.q: products (id, name, supplier_id, supplier_phone) has the key id. What is wrong with it?
questions.explain: That is a transitive dependency: id → supplier_id → supplier_phone. The supplier's phone would be repeated on every one of their products, with the same update anomaly as Ada's phone. Move it into suppliers.
options: It breaks 1NF because a phone is not atomic
It breaks 2NF because the key is composite
It breaks 3NF: supplier_phone depends on supplier_id, a non-key column, not on the product
Nothing, as long as supplier_id is a foreign key

questions.q: Which design breaks first normal form?
questions.explain: phone1, phone2, phone3 is a repeating group. It also caps customers at three phones and makes "find the customer with this phone" check three columns. A customer_phones table fixes both.
options: order_lines (order_id, product_id, quantity)
customers (id, name, phone1, phone2, phone3)
categories (id, parent_id, name)
payments (id, order_id, amount_kobo)

questions.q: Order lines store unit_price_kobo, although products.price_kobo exists. Is this a normalisation mistake?
questions.explain: If the rice price goes up next month, last month's orders must keep their totals. The line's price depends on the whole line (this order, this product, at that time), so it is correctly stored there.
options: Yes: the price must be read from products with a join
Yes, but it is needed for speed
No: it is a different fact, the price at the moment of sale, which must not change when the product price changes later
No, because generated columns can copy it automatically

questions.q: A product can be in several categories and a category holds many products. Where does the relationship live?
questions.explain: Many-to-many needs a third table with one row per link. The composite primary key stops the same link being stored twice, and both columns can be foreign keys.
options: A category_id column on products
A product_ids text column on categories
A join table product_categories (product_id, category_id) with both columns as the primary key
A jsonb column on both tables

questions.q: Why does the shop use id integer generated always as identity as the primary key of products, plus unique on sku, instead of making sku the primary key?
questions.explain: Natural keys change more often than expected. A meaningless surrogate key never needs to change, and the unique constraint on sku still prevents duplicates.
options: Because text columns cannot be primary keys
Because SKUs can change, and a changing primary key must be changed in every table that references it
Because unique is faster than primary key
Because identity columns are required for foreign keys

questions.q: Which on delete rule fits the foreign key from order_lines.product_id to products?
questions.explain: Cascading would silently delete sales history, and set null would leave lines that cannot say what was sold. Restrict refuses the delete; the shop marks such products as discontinued instead.
options: on delete cascade, so no orphan lines remain
on delete set null, so the line stays but forgets the product
on delete restrict, so a product that appears in sales history cannot be deleted
No foreign key at all, so products can be deleted freely

questions.q: You split a table into three and want to prove the split lost nothing. What does the lesson's check do?
questions.explain: A lossless decomposition gives back exactly the original rows when joined. A except B lists rows only in A; empty in both directions means no row was lost and none was invented.
options: Compares the number of columns before and after
Runs analyze on the new tables
Joins the new tables back together and uses except in both directions; both results must be empty
Checks that every new table has a primary key

questions.q: An order has two lines and two payments. A report joins orders to order_lines and payments in one query and sums line_total_kobo. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: This is fan-out: joining two independent child tables multiplies their rows. Aggregate each child table separately (a subquery or a grouped CTE per table), then combine the results.
options: Nothing, joins never change sums
Each line is paired with each payment, giving four rows, so the line total is counted twice
The query fails because two tables cannot be joined to one
Only the first payment is used

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two lines times two payments is four joined rows. Each line total appears twice and each payment appears twice, so both sums are doubled: 2 × 5,000 = 10,000.
options: { lines: 5000, paid: 5000 }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A plain unique compares text exactly, so a different capitalisation is a different value and Ada gets a second account. A unique index on lower(email) would have refused both.
options:
saved Ada@Example.com
23505 ada@example.com

23505 Ada@Example.com
23505 ada@example.com

saved Ada@Example.com
saved ada@example.com

23514 Ada@Example.com
23505 ada@example.com

questions.q: The phone column is unique but nullable. What does this print?
questions.explain: By default, nulls are not equal to each other, so a unique constraint allows any number of them. If "at most one missing phone" were the rule, PostgreSQL 15+ supports unique nulls not distinct.
options: The insert fails with 23505

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A stored generated column is recomputed on every insert and update of its row, so after the update it is 3 × 950,000. It can never drift from the columns it is computed from.
options: null

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Deleting category 10 cascades to its two links, (1, 10) and (2, 10). Products are untouched; only the link rows go. A link without its category means nothing, so cascade is right here.
options: [ { product_id: 1, category_id: 20 } ]
[ { product_id: 1, category_id: 20 }, { product_id: 2, category_id: 10 } ]
The delete fails with 23503

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Customer 2 has no orders, so nothing stops the delete. Customer 1 has order 100, and on delete restrict refuses with SQLSTATE 23001 (restrict violation). Financial records keep their customer.
options:
deleted 2 1
refused 1 23001

deleted 2 1
deleted 1 1

refused 2 23001
refused 1 23001

deleted 2 1
deleted 1 0

questions.q: What does this recursive query print?
questions.explain: The anchor gives 1. Each round adds i + 1 for the rows of the previous round while i < 4: 2, 3, 4. When i is 4 the recursive part returns nothing and the recursion stops. Four rows, 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.
options: { rows: 4, total: 10 }
{ rows: 3, total: 6 }
{ rows: 5, total: 15 }
{ rows: 1, total: 1 }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The anchor starts at Electronics (depth 0). Its children are Accessories and Audio (depth 1), and Chargers is below Accessories (depth 2). Groceries is a separate root, so it is not in this subtree.
options: { nodes: 4, deepest: 2 }
{ nodes: 5, deepest: 2 }
{ nodes: 3, deepest: 1 }
{ nodes: 4, deepest: 3 }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The check only compares a row with itself, so it stops a category being its own parent. Moving 1 under 3 creates the longer loop 1 → 3 → 2 → 1, which no single-row check can see. That needs a check in the code that moves categories, or a trigger.
options:
refused 3 under 3: 23514
moved 1 under 3

refused 3 under 3: 23514
refused 1 under 3: 23514

moved 3 under 3
moved 1 under 3

refused 3 under 3: 23503
moved 1 under 3

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A materialized view stores the result from when it was created or last refreshed. The second insert is invisible until refresh materialized view runs the query again.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly, in PostgreSQL just as in JavaScript. numeric is exact decimal arithmetic, and integer kobo is exact too. Money belongs in one of the last two.
options: { float_ok: false, numeric_ok: true, kobo_ok: true }
{ float_ok: true, numeric_ok: true, kobo_ok: true }
{ float_ok: false, numeric_ok: false, kobo_ok: true }
{ float_ok: true, numeric_ok: false, kobo_ok: true }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: group by sku folds the two earbud links into one row, and string_agg joins their categories with the separator you give, in the order you ask for inside the call.
options:
BUDS-01 2 Accessories|Audio
CHG-20W 1 Chargers

BUDS-01 2 Audio|Accessories
CHG-20W 1 Chargers

BUDS-01 1 Audio
BUDS-01 1 Accessories
CHG-20W 1 Chargers

BUDS-01 2 Accessories,Audio
CHG-20W 1 Chargers

questions.q: The order list page is slow. When is adding a cached orders.total_kobo column the right move?
questions.explain: Denormalisation trades write complexity and drift risk for faster reads. Do it deliberately: measure first, try an index, then write the value in the same transaction as the lines and run a reconciliation query.
options: Always: cached totals are best practice
Before launch, to be safe
After measuring that computing totals is the slow part, an index did not fix it, and you have a plan to keep the copy correct and detect drift
Never: denormalisation is always a mistake

questions.q: What is a reconciliation check?
questions.explain: Caches derived from other rows can drift when some code path forgets to update them. A query that compares cache and source, with an alert when it returns rows, catches that drift.
options: A constraint that refuses writes which would make a cached value wrong
A query, run regularly, that lists rows whose cached value disagrees with the data it was derived from
A command that refreshes a materialized view
A foreign key between the cache and the source

questions.q: What does cycle id set is_cycle using visited add to a recursive CTE?
questions.explain: The clause protects the read from looping forever. It does not stop bad data being written; the code that moves categories must still refuse loops.
options: It makes the query run the recursion in parallel
It forbids parent_id from ever pointing at a descendant
It tracks the ids seen on each path, marks a row whose id repeats with is_cycle = true, and stops expanding it
It limits recursion to one level

questions.q: What is the main trade-off of storing a category tree as an adjacency list (parent_id on each row)?
questions.explain: Only the moved node's parent_id changes, which makes writes simple. Reading all descendants needs with recursive. Materialised paths and closure tables flip that trade-off.
options: Moving a subtree requires updating every descendant
Moving a subtree is one update, but reading a whole subtree needs a recursive query
It cannot represent more than two levels
It needs a separate table for every level

questions.q: When is it reasonable to keep data in a jsonb column instead of rows in a table?
questions.explain: The lesson's rule of thumb: if you will filter by it, join on it, count it or constrain it, it deserves rows. A provider's raw webhook payload, stored for auditing, is a good fit for jsonb.
options: When you need foreign keys to the values
When you will count and filter by the values in most reports
When the data is free-form or kept as received, and you will not join, constrain or aggregate by its parts
Whenever it saves creating a table

questions.q: A comments (target_type, target_id) table points at orders or products. What is the main problem?
questions.explain: A foreign key references one table. With a type column, the database cannot enforce the link, and deleting an order leaves orphan comments. Use one nullable foreign key column per target with a check that exactly one is set, or one table per target.
options: It breaks 1NF
No foreign key can check target_id, so comments can point at rows that do not exist
PostgreSQL cannot index two columns together
It needs with recursive to read

questions.q: A developer proposes attributes (product_id, key, value text) "so we never need to change the schema". What does the shop lose?
questions.explain: Entity-attribute-value moves the schema into data, where the database cannot check it: every value is text, and "products under ₦5,000 in stock" becomes several self-joins. Add real columns with migrations, or a jsonb column for truly free-form extras.
options: Nothing, it is the most flexible design
Types and constraints on every value, and simple queries: each read becomes a pivot over key/value rows
Only some disk space
The ability to delete products

questions.q: Which rule can a single-row check constraint enforce?
questions.explain: A check sees only the row being written. reserved <= on_hand is inside one row. The others span several rows or tables, so they need transactions and application code, triggers, or invariant queries in tests.
options: An order has at least one line when it is paid
A customer may only review products they bought
Reserved stock never exceeds stock on hand in the same inventory row
The sum of succeeded payments never exceeds the order total

questions.q: Why does the lesson's schema test assert the SQLSTATE code (such as 23514) rather than just "an error happened"?
questions.explain: A test that accepts any error passes when the SQL itself is broken. Pinning the code proves the intended constraint did the refusing, and it pins the codes your HTTP error mapping depends on.
options: Because error messages are translated
Because the code says which rule refused the data; any error, even a typo in the test SQL, would pass an "any error" test
Because PostgreSQL does not always throw
Because the code is shorter to print

questions.q: Which type should orders.placed_at use?
questions.explain: timestamptz stores an absolute moment and converts correctly for any time zone. timestamp without a zone stores a wall-clock reading whose meaning depends on where it was written.
options: text, formatted as ISO 8601
timestamp (without time zone)
timestamptz
integer seconds, always

questions.q: If you choose UUIDs for primary keys, why prefer a time-ordered kind such as UUIDv7?
questions.explain: A B-tree index stays compact and cache-friendly when new keys arrive in order. Random UUIDs scatter inserts across the whole index. The next lesson looks inside B-trees.
options: They are shorter than random UUIDs
New keys sort after old ones, so inserts land at the end of the index instead of at random places
They are guaranteed never to collide, unlike random UUIDs
They can be used as foreign keys, unlike random UUIDs

questions.q: Bring a packed column into first normal form. Write toLines(orderId, items) that turns "RICE-5KG x2, OIL-1L x1" into one object per item: { orderId, sku, quantity } with a number quantity. Accept any amount of space around the commas.
questions.explain: Split on the comma alone and trim each piece, so the spacing does not matter. Each item becomes its own row, which is what an order_lines table stores.

questions.q: Before moving the sheet into a customers table, find contradictions. Write phoneConflicts(rows) that returns the emails that appear with more than one different phone, sorted.
questions.explain: Group phones by email in a Set, so repeats of the same phone count once. Any email with more than one distinct phone is a contradiction the normalised table would refuse; in SQL: group by email having count(distinct phone) > 1.

questions.q: Write breadcrumb(categories, id) that follows parentId upwards and returns the names from the root down, joined with " / ". It is the JavaScript version of the "up" recursive CTE.
questions.explain: A Map by id makes each step up a constant-time lookup. unshift puts each parent in front, so the root ends up first, like string_agg(name, ' / ' order by level desc).

questions.q: Stop loops before they are written. Write canMove(categories, id, newParentId): it returns false if newParentId is the category itself or any of its descendants, otherwise true. Walk up from the new parent.
questions.explain: If walking up from the new parent ever reaches the category being moved, the new parent is inside its subtree and the move would create a loop. Walking up is cheap: one step per level.

questions.q: Compute each order's total and paid amount without fan-out. Write summary(lines, payments) returning { orderId, totalKobo, paidKobo } per order that has lines, sorted by order id. Only payments with status "succeeded" count.
questions.explain: Aggregate each child collection on its own, then combine per order. Pairing every line with every payment first would double both sums, which is the fan-out bug from the lesson.

questions.q: Write the reconciliation check in JavaScript: drift(orders, lines) returns the ids of orders whose cached totalKobo differs from the sum of their lines' lineTotalKobo (an order with no lines should total 0).
questions.explain: Order 3's lines add up to 3,350,000, not the cached 1,450,000, and order 4 has no lines at all but a cached 500. The SQL version needs a left join (or a subquery with coalesce) for the same reason: orders without lines must be checked too.

questions.q: Before adding a unique index on lower(email), find the rows that would break it. Write caseDuplicates(emails) that returns groups (arrays) of emails that are equal when lower-cased, only groups with more than one entry.
questions.explain: Group by the same expression the index will use. Creating the unique index on dirty data fails with 23505, so real migrations find and merge these accounts first. In SQL: group by lower(email) having count(*) > 1.

questions.q: Print a category tree from an adjacency list: roots first, each child indented two spaces per level, siblings sorted by name. Use recursion.
questions.explain: The recursion is depth-first: print a node, then its whole subtree, then the next sibling. The recursive CTE got the same order by sorting on the built-up path.
